claims.text: Increasing lattice-parameter mismatch across FCC/BCC HEA multilayer interfaces changes the nucleation of misfit dislocations.
Increasing lattice-parameter mismatch changes dislocation transmission across the interfaces.
Misfit-dislocation nucleation and transmission govern progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading.
The proposed starting multilayers have FCC CoCrFeMnNi layers paired with a BCC alloy such as FeCrMoNb.
The starting multilayers have nominally lattice-matched interfaces.
Compositional tuning can introduce a controlled interfacial lattice-parameter mismatch.
Introducing controlled lattice mismatch promotes misfit-dislocation formation.
Compositional complexity and severe lattice distortion in HEAs facilitate heterogeneous nucleation of misfit dislocations at interfaces.
A sufficient but non-excessive lattice mismatch causes earlier dislocation nucleation.
Interfacial misfit dislocations act as rate-limiting barriers to subsequent dislocation transmission.
The barrier effect of interfacial misfit dislocations slows subsequent plastic deformation.
Nominally matched interfaces have weaker barriers to dislocation transmission than deliberately mismatched interfaces.
Controlled-mismatch multilayers will begin plastic flow at lower strain or shorter creep time than nominally matched multilayers.
After dislocation activation, controlled-mismatch multilayers will have a lower creep rate than nominally matched multilayers.
Excessive lattice mismatch may cause premature failure.
The proposed behavior applies to nanoscale multilayer coatings tested at 300–400 °C under fixed load.
Temperatures outside 300–400 °C or extreme mismatch may activate additional mechanisms, including diffusion-controlled deformation.
